title: Trump Touts Baby Bonds in Georgia, But Delays and Criticism Cloud the Rollout
summary:
President Trump took his pitch for Trump Accounts—a $1,000 government-funded investment account for every child born during his term—to a Georgia high school on Wednesday, framing it as a way to lift kids out of poverty and give all Americans a stake in the stock market. But as he spoke, some parents were still refreshing their bank apps, waiting for the promised seed money to land.

The accounts, launched July 4, are a centerpiece of Trump's signature One Big Beautiful Bill. They're open to any child under 18, but the $1,000 kickstart is reserved for babies born from 2025 through 2028. The Treasury Department says 6.5 million have enrolled, with 1.5 million eligible for the seed funding. The money is invested in index funds by private firms and can't be accessed until age 18, and only for education, homeownership, or starting a business.

But the rollout has been bumpy. Masaki and Kristina McLellan of Bergen County, New Jersey, applied for their newborn Maya on July 6. After an initial rejection and an hour-long call to the hotline, they were told to expect the money in 10 days—then up to four weeks. "It's disappointing," Kristina said, though Maya already has a 529 college plan and a custodial brokerage account. The Treasury calls the lag "standard processing time, like receiving a tax refund," and says most parents wait just one to two days.

The program has drawn fire from anti-poverty advocates who note it does nothing for children in their earliest, most vulnerable years. The same bill that created Trump Accounts also slashed funding for Medicaid and SNAP, programs disproportionately used by kids. Supporters argue it's a bold move to counter the appeal of democratic socialists and give every child a foothold in capitalism. With Trump's economic approval at just 33%, the Georgia stop was as much about midterm messaging as it was about baby bonds.
why_it_matters: This program will shape how the U.S. helps families build wealth—it could become a permanent part of the social safety net or a cautionary tale if the promised money doesn't arrive on time. For teenagers, it’s a real-world example of a heated debate: should government invest in future assets like savings accounts, or protect immediate needs like food and healthcare?

background_read: President Donald Trump, who returned to office in January 2025 after winning the 2024 election, has put “baby bonds” at the center of his domestic agenda. The idea of a government-funded savings account for every newborn was popularized by economists to reduce wealth inequality and has been proposed in the U.S. Congress before, but never enacted until now.

The Trump Accounts were created as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill, a wide-ranging law that also made large cuts to safety-net programs. Medicaid (the joint federal-state health insurance program for low-income patients) and SNAP (the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, once known as food stamps) saw reduced funding, drawing strong criticism from anti-poverty groups.

The rollout echoes past government aid programs that faced delays and confusion, such as the early days of the Affordable Care Act website. The Treasury Department manages the accounts and compares processing times to tax refunds, but critics argue that a program meant to help from day one shouldn't leave families waiting while other supports are taken away.

perspectives.description: Families with newborns see a chance to give their children a financial head start that will grow with the economy. Advocates believe the accounts will teach financial literacy and spread stock ownership more widely, giving a sense of shared prosperity. They argue it's a positive alternative to just handing out welfare.

Opponents point out that cutting SNAP and Medicaid hurts the same children the Trump Accounts are supposed to help—and the damage begins long before age 18. They see a cruel trade-off: a promise of future wealth while hunger and healthcare needs go unaddressed now. The delays in paying the seed money make it hard to trust the government's commitment.

perspectives.perspective: Analysts and historians of social policy
perspectives.description: The Trump Accounts reflect a longer trend in Republican policy from direct aid to asset-building. Similar ideas like Child Trust Funds in the UK had mixed results. The funding model—pairing new benefits with cuts to established safety nets—mirrors previous political compromises that often left the most vulnerable without a net.

If the accounts stabilize and delays end, they could become a normal part of growing up, potentially expanding to include older children. But legal challenges over funding cuts and ongoing criticism could force revisions. The program's success or failure at the ballot box in the next midterm elections will determine whether baby bonds remain a policy or become a relic.
